title: Learned Hand's Shlomo Klapper on Why Courts Are the Next Frontier for Legal AI
author: Shlomo Klapper

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Klapper’s account supports the practical value of specialist legal software through substantial reported research acceleration and strong lawyer demand. However, he also argues that capabilities once distinctive to Casetext are now available through general-purpose AI tools at essentially no cost, directly qualifying the cluster’s thesis that specialist workflow layers can defend durable value. He does not address contextual integration, verification or governance.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s workflow-and-implementation framing into courts: it describes an exploratory partnership spanning filing through drafting and highlights that cheaper legal services may increase filings and judicial workload. Its claims remain prospective and provide no measured outcomes, reinforcing the cluster’s caution against treating announced capabilities as demonstrated transformation.
qs: Learned Hand just announced a partnership with the Superior Court of Los Angeles County, the largest trial court in the nation, to explore how AI can support judicial officers across the full arc of a case from filing through drafting.

In our conversation today, Shlomo and I discuss why courts are the next frontier for legal AI, what it takes to earn the trust of judges, and how Jevons Paradox, the idea that as legal services get cheaper, demand will explode, is reshaping the justice system.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Klapper accepts the cluster’s core human-led, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it to courts. He identifies judicial tasks where AI should assist rather than decide, specifies programmatic verification throughout complex legal workflows, and proposes deliberate friction to prevent passive deference—concrete design safeguards for high-consequence use.
qs: um so I think that the big question is about sentencing, which I think is extremely problematic for a machine to do sentencing and extremely imperative to machine to assist with sensitive meaning there's a tool called one of my bet.
where we're processing the information in such a way and then doing verification steps in all along the way.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: Klapper supports the cluster’s emphasis on earned trust and caution toward unsupported technology claims. He frames technology providers as responsible for earning judicial trust rather than assuming it, while offering no empirical outcomes or concrete validation measures. The source therefore reinforces, but does not materially extend, the cluster’s proposition.
qs: Silicon Valley and our next conversation, we can talk about how Silicon Valley has completely, why people shouldn't trust it and why we have, as tech people need to earn the trust rather than just assume it.
We're here to help rather than just something that's a shiny new.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: Klapper supports assessing judicial AI against courts’ existing capacity constraints rather than an idealised human process. He presents AI as decision support, not judicial replacement, and aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on factual verification, provenance and demonstrated time savings, while offering no measured pilot outcomes on accuracy or fairness.
qs: So there's simply not enough ways, time to read everything.
And we have to show that we can deeply verify every single fact that we have a chain of provenance that it double checks it and that it actually can save you time.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Klapper supports the cluster’s core copilot-not-autopilot proposition: AI should assist with bounded epistemic tasks while consequential legal decisions remain with accountable humans. His court-focused argument does not materially address the cluster’s broader claims about pricing, staffing or provider restructuring, but it reinforces the limits of autonomous legal delivery, especially in high-stakes settings.
qs: So in my view is that I want the machines helping with the epistemic tasks and not making any constitutive decisions.

We haven't built that yet, but I do think that even in these very, very sensitive uh situations, and I would argue especially in those sensitive decisions, even if we don't want the machine making the decision, I don't want the machine making that decision, but I would want the judges to have the best tools available to assist them in these crucial, crucial life and death situations.

kp.k: Cheaper litigation could overwhelm fixed judicial capacity
kp.d: Klapper applies Jevons paradox to predict that falling litigation costs will increase case volumes, while courts cannot readily increase judge numbers or refuse cases. This is his forward-looking rationale for court-focused AI, not a quantified forecast. He also asserts that 90% of judges lack a dedicated clerk.
qs: But that means cases are going to go up.
Courts have a fixed number of judges and they can't turn away cases.
And by the way, 90 % of judges don't have a clerk, dedicated clerk, so they're doing all this work themselves.

kp.k: Access gains require corresponding investment in court capacity
kp.d: Klapper argues that affordable AI-assisted litigation can help people protect housing, pursue custody and challenge more powerful parties. He acknowledges that AI can make frivolous filings appear credible and harder to debunk, but favors expanding access alongside judicial capacity rather than restricting litigants' tools. His description of an unauthorized-practice lawsuit against OpenAI as frivolous is his opinion.
qs: People can stop being evicted from their homes. People can fight for custody of their children.
So it takes longer to debunk untrue things.
But we need to be able to increase capacity on the court side because otherwise you have bots versus bots and the humans are going to caught in the middle.

kp.k: Judicial AI should assist rather than replace judgment
kp.d: Klapper positions Learned Hand as an AI law clerk that organizes information and supports judges, clerks and staff attorneys. He grounds the augmentation boundary in institutional legitimacy: a technology company has not been elected or authorized to make judicial decisions. His account emphasizes relieving workload while retaining judicial responsibility.
qs: So what we're building is, I like to call it a judicial sous chef. We're not replacing the judgment part.
We are in essence like an AI law clerk.
They're not replacing the judge.

kp.k: Judicial neutrality demands tools distinct from advocacy software
kp.d: Klapper argues that general-purpose AI's tendency to agree with users fits advocacy more readily than adjudication. He says Learned Hand is designed to identify factual differences, missing documents and analytical gaps. He reports a White & Case study showing 90% lawyer approval of lawyers using AI versus approximately 24% approval of judges using it, and invokes the EU AI Act's high-risk treatment of adjudication; neither claim is independently documented in the transcript.
qs: For judges, this is anathema because the judge's goal is to find the truth, to figure out what's actually happening.
It will say, I generated this, but I'm missing x or y documents. You might want to look into this. Here are the gaps of the analysis.
And lawyers approving of judges using AI, like 24%.

kp.k: Court workflows extend from record navigation to draft orders
kp.d: Klapper describes a modular workbench offering brief-to-record hyperlinks, checks of whether cited sources support lawyers' assertions, record queries with pinpoint citations, research, bench memoranda and draft orders. He identifies Midpage and Open Laws as research sources. Adoption can stop at navigation or research; analysis and drafting are optional, and one court requested no recommendations.
qs: it's a workbench. It's a series of tools that assist judges from filing to the first draft.
One of the ways in which we do that is we're able to take the briefs and hyperlink them to the record.
partner with a company called Midpage, which I absolutely love.
We have access to statutes for open laws, which is another company that I love.
one court that's trying us out, they requested like a no recommendation feature.

kp.k: Bias reduction claims rest on reported tests and anecdotes
kp.d: Klapper reports that an unnamed core partner tested Learned Hand by changing names, genders and other background characteristics in otherwise unchanged cases, finding no evidence of bias. No sample size, detailed methodology or numerical results are supplied. He also recounts a bench memorandum challenging his own anti-plaintiff assumptions, presenting AI as a potentially corrective second perspective rather than establishing generally unbiased performance.
qs: They took a bunch of cases, they swapped out the names and genders, et cetera, and then they threw it through the machine, our machine at learn hand.
There was actually no evidence of bias.
I am saying though, that it can help not just make things more efficient, it can also assist with making things fairer.

kp.k: Deliberate friction may protect independent judicial reasoning
kp.d: Asked whether generated analysis could anchor judges, Klapper initially emphasizes their skepticism and says none he has spoken with has relinquished control. He nevertheless acknowledges he may be wrong, particularly for newer judges, and describes work with one judge on a proposed 'hard mode' that asks questions instead of simply providing a finished answer. This is an exploratory safeguard, not an evaluated intervention.
qs: not a single one of them has abdicated control to it.
I also recognize that I might be wrong in this stand, especially for newer judges.
it's just raising the questions, forcing you to think, and having deliberate friction in the process.

kp.k: Hallucination controls combine automated checking and programmatic constraints
kp.d: Klapper says most LLM expenditure goes to what he calls verification: automated clause-level checking through numerous parallel model calls, traffic-light flags and regeneration. He describes a shift toward programmatic processing and checks throughout the workflow, while acknowledging the difficulty of using unreliable models to check other models. These are vendor claims about automated safeguards, distinct from human verification before reliance; no measured error rate is supplied.
qs: The vast majority of our LLM costs are based on verification, not on generation.
And you basically run a thousand parallel, LLM calls, even multiple.
how do you have something untrustworthy, checking something that's already untrustworthy?
What lends itself much more to verification is relying on things that are code, regular expressions, identity recognitions, et cetera, a lot more of that on the ex-ante side.

kp.k: Los Angeles rollout uses staged, motion-specific evaluation
kp.d: The host identifies the announced Los Angeles Superior Court pilot as civil-only. Klapper says the court initially evaluated difficult motions with an extensive multipart, one-to-five quality rubric, including a head-to-head comparison against an unnamed multibillion-dollar research company. He claims Learned Hand won decisively but supplies no scores or test sample size. He describes subsequent testing by six judges and six staff attorneys, with motion-specific release to the wider court conditional on passing evaluation.
qs: And I insisted on the hardest motions.
one to five on levels of quality of certain dimensions.
So we had a head-to-head competition with us and this multi-billion dollar company evaluating it.
six judges, six staff attorneys testing every going motion by motion.

kp.k: Summary judgment illustrates claimed judicial time savings
kp.d: Klapper describes linking statements of undisputed material facts to evidence, assessing disputedness and materiality against claim elements, and checking evidentiary objections. He relays judges' reports of tasks shrinking from four hours to 10 minutes and motions from three hours to five minutes. These are vendor-carried customer reports, not controlled productivity findings; he proposes spending recovered time on hearings, deeper analysis and faster resolution.
qs: It will do an analysis of the disputedness and materiality.
But then you have to make sure that you link to the elements of the claim, right?
the responses we're getting from judges is that it would take things that would take them four hours and turn it to 10 minutes. A motion that would take three hours and turn it to five minutes.

kp.k: Criminal applications require boundaries around state-authorized decisions
kp.d: Klapper identifies suppression and post-conviction motions as suitable assistance tasks, while distinguishing epistemic questions from constitutive decisions whose authority comes from judges and the state. He rejects machine sentencing and criticizes COMPAS as encouraging deference to opaque recommendations. He proposes, but says he has not built, sentencing assistance that retrieves similar cases or acts as a devil's advocate; he would remove recommendations if deference became a problem.
qs: post-conviction relief is a big motion, suppression motions are uh big and those are ones we help with and that cleanly fits.
I want the machines helping with the epistemic tasks and not making any constitutive decisions.
So instead of making a sensitive decision, how about a machine that would pull up similar cases?
We haven't built that yet

kp.k: Court incentives differ from hourly legal practice
kp.d: Klapper argues that courts' incentives favor efficiency without the billable-hour constraint facing legal-practice customers. He presents this as an advantage of selling to judges, not as evidence that law firms have changed pricing models. Asked about pricing and financing, he discusses market creation and investment rather than disclosing a price or contractual model.
qs: one of the benefits of serving judges is that the incentives are completely aligned
They're not limited by any sort of billable hour.

kp.k: Court software market dominance is a speculative investment thesis
kp.d: Using Palantir's intelligence-software category creation as an analogy, Klapper predicts that courts will create budgets for effective AI and that adjudication software will become a winner-take-all market. He cites structural barriers, network effects, founder specialization and a market small enough to dominate, alongside predicted litigation growth. These are commercial expectations, not demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: They were able to create the category that then they dominate.
The budgets will be created for them.
because of the structural barriers, because I'm a one-of-one founder, because of the network effects, because it's a small enough market to dominate.
the amount of cases we're going to see is going to explode.

kp.k: Institutional trust is central to adoption
kp.d: Klapper describes judges as both skeptical and curious, with adoption requiring demonstrations of accuracy, provenance, safety and time savings, followed by reassurance that the tool does not displace their role. He presents respect for judicial institutions and collaborative development, informed by his Palantir experience, as essential to earning trust rather than assuming it.
qs: we have to show that we can deeply verify every single fact that we have a chain of provenance that it double checks it and that it actually can save you time.
It's both safe and effective.
I'm saying I'm not here to disrupt, I'm here to build and build together.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Klapper predicts that cheaper AI-enabled litigation will expand access and case volumes, making judicial capacity the next bottleneck.
pts.d: Shlomo Klapper argues that falling litigation costs will increase demand under Jevons paradox. He welcomes greater access for people with otherwise uneconomic claims, including housing and custody disputes, while acknowledging that more polished frivolous filings take longer to debunk. Because courts cannot refuse cases and cannot expand judicial staffing sufficiently quickly, he predicts that they will need AI assistance to manage growing workloads. His claim concerns both unmet individual legal need and the resulting institutional burden, rather than simply enterprise cost savings.

pts.k: Klapper presents judicial AI as an assistant that can improve speed, depth and preparation without replacing judicial judgment.
pts.d: He says Learned Hand organizes records, hyperlinks briefs to underlying evidence, flags unsupported characterizations, provides research and querying, and generates bench memoranda and draft orders. For summary judgment, he describes analysis of disputedness, materiality, claim elements and evidentiary objections. He reports substantial time savings and argues that judges can redirect that time toward hearings, deeper analysis and faster resolution. This is an augmentation claim: the judge retains decision-making authority even where the tool supplies analysis or a draft.

pts.k: Klapper claims courts need purpose-built, neutral AI rather than tools optimized for advocacy, and that such tools may improve fairness.
pts.d: He contrasts generic generative AI's tendency to agree with users with the judicial need to examine competing accounts neutrally. He says Learned Hand identifies missing documents and analytical gaps, and can challenge a human reader's predispositions. He argues that machine outputs can be audited for bias and that an additional analytical perspective can make adjudication fairer as well as more efficient. He does not claim that judges should delegate decisions to the system.

pts.k: Klapper claims robust source checking and increasingly programmatic safeguards can improve the reliability of judicial AI.
pts.d: He describes clause-level automated checking using parallel model calls, traffic-light indications of support, and regeneration of flagged material. He says the company is shifting toward programmatic processing and checks because these have produced its best accuracy, particularly for quotations and key facts. He argues that a closed source collection alone is insufficient and that similar safeguards would benefit lawyer-facing products. The transcript calls these automated processes 'verification'; it does not describe a measured reduction in the human work required to verify AI output before reliance.

pts.k: Klapper advocates AI assistance, but not machine decision-making, in criminal sentencing and other exercises of judicial authority.
pts.d: He distinguishes epistemic tasks—answering factual or legal questions—from constitutive decisions in which judicial authority determines the outcome. Sentencing exemplifies the latter and, in his account, lacks democratic legitimacy if delegated to a machine. He nevertheless argues that especially consequential decisions warrant better AI support, such as finding similar cases or testing a judge's reasoning. He identifies suppression and post-conviction motions as existing applications, while describing real-time trial work as less suited to the current product.

pts.k: Klapper predicts a large, concentrated market for judicial AI, with new public budgets created in response to demonstrated efficiency.
pts.d: He argues that courts' incentives align with efficiency because they do not depend on billable hours. He characterizes judicial AI as a category-creation opportunity analogous to Palantir's intelligence software market, rather than an inherently small market constrained by current software budgets. He predicts that increasing adjudication demand, structural entry barriers and network effects will favor a dominant provider. These are commercial forecasts by the company's founder; he does not supply pricing, revenue or quantified market-size projections.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The support consists principally of Klapper's professional experience, customer feedback, a reported partner bias study and a reported court evaluation; the transcript supplies no underlying datasets or full results.
pts.d: For efficiency, Klapper reports judges' before-and-after time estimates, rather than presenting a controlled productivity study. His clerkship story—a week of detailed review contributing to a ten-year sentence reduction—illustrates the value of more analytical time but is not evidence of an AI outcome. For fairness, he reports an unnamed court partner's test that substituted names, genders and other backgrounds in cases and found no evidence of bias; sample size, metrics and results are not supplied. He also recounts a Southwest airport dispute in which an AI bench memorandum challenged his initial anti-plaintiff assessment. For output quality, he says Los Angeles evaluated difficult motions using an extensive rubric and compared Learned Hand with an unnamed large legal research company's product; he reports a decisive advantage but gives no scores or test-set details. For reliability, he describes engineering methods and expresses confidence in quotation and fact accuracy without reporting an error rate. For growing demand and market concentration, he offers economic reasoning and analogies, not quantified forecasts. His accounts of judicial workload and insufficient clerk support provide contextual motivation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current product and pilot claims are distinct from conditional court-wide rollout, features under development and largely undated market forecasts.
pts.d: At the time of the 2026 interview, Klapper describes existing court use and an initial Los Angeles comparative evaluation followed by motion-specific testing by approximately six judges and six staff attorneys. Wider release to hundreds of court personnel is contingent on passing evaluation for each motion type; comprehensive coverage remains an aspiration. Adoption is modular: judges may use only hyperlinks, summaries or research, and one court requested no recommendations. He acknowledges possible overreliance, particularly among newer judges, and is exploring a 'hard mode' that introduces questions and deliberate friction. Review of judges' own work is a forthcoming feature, and proposed sentencing-specific comparison and challenge tools have not yet been built. His reliability claims require continuing vigilance and layered safeguards, not complacency. Predictions of exploding demand and new budget lines have no numerical horizon; his explicit commercial horizon is that supportive investors will look prescient in three years.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are judges and court staff, individual litigants, advocates whose submissions are checked, and judicial-AI suppliers and public funders.
pts.d: Judges, clerks and staff attorneys—especially in understaffed state trial courts and document-heavy motions practice—are the direct users, gaining research, preparation and drafting capacity rather than being replaced. Klapper describes applicability across civil, family, trial-criminal and some probate work, with particularly sensitive limits in sentencing. Self-represented and otherwise underserved litigants may obtain practical access to courts, while all litigants depend on courts being able to process the additional demand without losing trust or timeliness. Lawyers face more systematic checking of factual and legal characterizations in their briefs. Courts and public funders are expected to create technology budgets; Learned Hand and competing suppliers face a market Klapper predicts will concentrate around a dominant provider. Criminal defendants and others subject to coercive judicial decisions are affected by both potential analytical improvements and the risks of deference to machine recommendations.
